This division stands under the national federal framework of this country; the national layer is carried on the national record rather than repeated here.

A national legal risk assessment published in July 2026 places this division in its Low-Risk group alongside eight other divisions, describing that group as jurisdictions that have largely refrained from targeting transgender adults. The same assessment names this division together with one other division as a jurisdiction whose youth-targeting anti-trans policies are judged unlikely to be extended to adults.

Employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity is prohibited in this division through 2020 federal appeals-court rulings under Title VII covering sexual orientation and gender identity, reinforced by a January 2023 gubernatorial executive order banning gender-identity discrimination in state employment and contracts and a June 2023 statement by the chief legal officer affirming that state sex discrimination includes gender identity. Municipal ordinances in nine municipalities (revised February 2013, March 2013, February 2014, 2015, November 2018, March 2021, April 2021 effective 20 May, May 2021 and June 2021) ban gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations, with exemptions for religious organizations, expressive groups, government agencies, private clubs and small businesses.

The division's hate-crime statute does not include gender identity, though a federal hate-crimes prevention act has covered gender identity since October 2009. A gay and trans panic defence remains available under common law, with reform bills lapsing without action.

Gender-affirming care for minors is restricted. A March 2022 law signed by the governor banned sex reassignment surgery on transgender children effective March 2023, with an exception permitting surgery on intersex children. A 1982 regulation bars public medical-assistance coverage of sex reassignment surgery; that ban was challenged in August 2020 by two transgender teenagers with national civil-rights and health-law co-counsel as unconstitutional, following 2019 lawsuits seeking to void it. A June 2023 executive order granted government employees over age 21 full public medical-assistance and insurance coverage for gender-affirming healthcare and services. Conversion therapy was banned in one county in August 2017 by a 3-2 vote with fines up to $2,500, alongside a June 2023 executive order barring government funding for conversion therapy.

The division's highest court ruled on 25 April 2019 that family courts may determine care for a transgender child with gender dysphoria only in limited circumstances when divorced parents reach impasse, authorized to decide disputed parenting-plan elements narrowly tailored on evidence of imminent harm. In March 2023 the division's education department introduced a hotline to report schools exposing children to topics including gender ideology for investigation. In June 2023 the governor vetoed legislature-passed anti-trans bathroom and classroom pronoun-usage bills and vetoed an April 2023 bill targeting LGBT safe spaces in schools.

A second March 2022 bill signed by the governor legally bars transgender children from female sports, athletics and Olympic competition, effective 30 days after enactment.

Birth certificates and driver's licences carry distinct rules. In November 2020 three families with transgender children sued the division's health authority to permit birth-certificate gender change without sex reassignment surgery; litigation was ongoing as of August 2023 with all resident transgender individuals joined, and an August 2024 federal judge order permitted change without surgery. Driver's licence and state ID gender change requires a signed physician statement attesting the applicant is irrevocably committed to the gender-change process, without requiring surgery.

Same-sex marriage has been recognized since a federal district court decision on 17 October 2014 ended enforcement of statutory and constitutional bans, though those bans remain textually in the division's constitution and statutory code as unenforceable under a 2015 highest-court marriage-equality ruling and, for out-of-state recognition, a 2022 federal marriage-recognition act. Voters rejected a 2006 ballot measure and approved a 2008 ballot measure banning recognition, prompting four municipalities to enact domestic partnerships or civil unions.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal after a 2001 repeal statute did away with sodomy laws. Adoption is permitted with no explicit prohibition on same-sex couples or second-parent adoptions, though primary consideration goes to married couples unless in the child's best interest or no married couple is available; the division's highest court ruled unanimously in September 2017 that same-sex spouses have equal parental rights under the 2015 marriage-equality ruling and a subsequent highest-court ruling to list both names on birth certificates, with October 2020 appeals implementation. Surrogacy contracts are unenforceable though a 1994 state appellate ruling allows pre-birth orders for biological parents requiring second-parent adoption for a non-biological same-sex parent, and an April 2022 emergency law signed by the governor allows religious organizations to legally discriminate against same-sex couples seeking to adopt or foster.

On 3 June 2026 a national monitoring project reported that the local pride organisation cancelled all 2026 events in January and effectively dissolved, citing a political and financial environment that made supporting queer events nearly impossible; that city was grouped with two cities in other divisions of this country as affected cities.

This division's position in the July 2026 national assessment's lowest-concern group reflects its relative restraint in targeting transgender adults, but the same assessment notes that this division has enacted youth-targeting anti-trans policies judged unlikely to be extended to adults — a distinction that may not hold if legislative priorities shift.

The cancellation and dissolution of a Pride event in this division's second-largest city in January 2026, reported by a publication on 3 June 2026, signals a deteriorating environment for visible LGBTQ organizing in that city, even where formal legal protections remain in place. That city was grouped with two cities in other divisions of this country as places where Pride events were affected.

This division's protections rest substantially on a patchwork: federal employment-law rulings, a 2023 executive order from the head of the division's government, a 2023 interpretation by the division's chief legal officer, and municipal ordinances in nine cities, each with religious, expressive, governmental, private-club and small-business exemptions. A change in the office of the head of government or of the chief legal officer could narrow the division-level layer without altering the federal or municipal ones.

This division's 1982 public health insurance exclusion for sex-reassignment surgery remains on the books despite the 2020 constitutional challenge and the June 2023 executive order extending coverage to public-sector employees over 21; the interaction between these instruments is not resolved in the sources.

This division's hate-crime statute does not cover gender identity, though this country's federal hate-crime prevention legislation has covered it since October 2009. A gay and trans panic defence remains available under this division's common law; reform bills have lapsed without action.

Driver's licence and state ID gender-marker change requires a signed physician statement attesting the applicant is irrevocably committed to the gender-change process, without requiring surgery. Birth-certificate gender change without surgery was permitted by an August 2024 federal judge order following litigation filed in November 2020 by three families with transgender children against this division's health department.

A March 2022 law signed by the governor bars sex reassignment surgery on transgender children effective March 2023, with an exception permitting surgery on intersex children. A second March 2022 bill signed by the governor bars transgender children from female sports, athletics and Olympic competition effective 30 days after enactment.

A 1982 regulation bars public health-insurance coverage of sex reassignment surgery; the ban was challenged in August 2020 by two transgender teenagers with a national legal advocacy organisation and co-counsel as unconstitutional, following 2019 lawsuits. A June 2023 executive order granted government employees over age 21 full public health-insurance access and insurance coverage for gender-affirming healthcare and services.

Conversion therapy was banned in one of the division's counties in August 2017 by a 3-2 vote with fines up to $2,500. A June 2023 executive order bars government funding for conversion therapy.

In March 2023 the division's education department introduced a hotline to report schools exposing children to topics including gender ideology for investigation. In June 2023 the governor vetoed legislature-passed anti-trans bathroom and classroom pronoun-usage bills and an April 2023 bill targeting LGBT safe spaces in schools.

Employment and public-accommodations protections apply through federal employment-discrimination court rulings (2020), a January 2023 gubernatorial executive order for state employment and contracts, a June 2023 attorney general affirmation that state sex discrimination includes gender identity, and nine municipal ordinances passed between February 2013 and June 2021 (February 2013; March 2013; February 2014; 2015; November 2018; March 2021; April 2021, effective 20 May; May 2021; June 2021), each with religious, expressive, governmental, private-club and small-business exemptions.

Same-sex marriage has been recognized since a federal district court decision on 17 October 2014 ended enforcement of statutory and constitutional bans, though bans remain textually in this division's constitution and statutes as unenforceable under this country's 2015 highest-court marriage-equality ruling and the 2022 federal marriage-respect act. Adoption carries no explicit prohibition on same-sex couples or second-parent adoptions; this country's highest civil court ruled unanimously in September 2017 that same-sex spouses have equal parental rights under the 2015 marriage-equality ruling and a 2017 follow-on ruling of that court to list both names on birth certificates, with October 2020 appeals implementation. Surrogacy contracts are unenforceable though a 1994 divisional court decision allows pre-birth orders for biological parents requiring second-parent adoption for a non-biological same-sex parent, and an April 2022 emergency law signed by the governor allows religious organisations to legally discriminate against same-sex couples seeking to adopt or foster.

The interaction between this division's 1982 public health insurance exclusion covering sex-reassignment surgery, the August 2020 constitutional challenge to it, and the June 2023 executive order extending gender-affirming coverage to employees of the division's government over 21 is unresolved in the sources; which instrument controls for a given patient is not stated.

The status of the November 2020 birth-certificate litigation after the August 2024 order of a federal judge is not documented in the inventory beyond that order; whether the ruling has been appealed or narrowed is unresolved.

The criteria used by the July 2026 assessment for this country to group jurisdictions, and for judging youth-targeting policies "unlikely to be extended to adults," are not detailed in the sources; the basis for that judgment is unresolved.

Whether the June 2023 executive order of the governor and the June 2023 interpretation by the chief legal officer survive a change of administration, and whether the municipal ordinances' exemptions have been litigated, is not sourced.

No incident in this division of trans-directed violence, arrest, or detention is documented in this inventory; the absence of such a record is not evidence that none has occurred.

The care-access law of this division is the most protective element of its own record. The serving governor signed the legislation in September 2022, making this division the first jurisdiction in this country to declare itself a sanctuary for transgender young people seeking medical care. Out-of-state youth can obtain hormones and puberty blockers here, and the law shields families from child-abuse investigations or criminal prosecution for seeking gender-affirming care, including families who travel to this division for it.

The prison system here is the one documented instance of identity-based placement in this inventory. As of January 2021 this division is coded as the single jurisdiction allowing transgender inmates to be housed according to their gender identity, with housing assigned identity-based within the general population and no trans-only separate facility documented. In 2015 this division became the first jurisdiction to fund gender-affirming surgeries for transgender prison inmates, and reporting from a broadcast outlet covering the operational guidelines of the prison service that year confirms the identity-based care and guidance posture while containing no explicit statement of a trans-only unit or segregation practice. The most recent documented statement of this housing practice in this record is dated January 2021; no later instance is documented.

Recorded hostility sits alongside that protective framework. An advocacy monitoring desk documented more than 1,000 anti-LGBTQ incidents across the country in 2025, of which this division recorded 198, the highest figure of any jurisdiction. That position is by raw count only: the source supplies no population or per-capita denominator, so the count does not establish that this division is riskier for an individual visitor than a smaller one.

A separate analysis of the same 2025 incident data reports a dramatic increase in anti-LGBTQ hate-crime reports in the largest city of this division in law-enforcement data covering the same period as the serving governor's platforming of anti-trans figures.

A July 2026 analysis places this division in a top-tier statutory-protection band with a recorded 1.9 incidents, and argues that even the most protective statutory floors do not eliminate recorded hostility.

The same 2025 national incident count that puts this division at 198 records one other division at 72, a second division at 66, and two further divisions at 50 each. The comparison is between raw counts across divisions of very different population sizes, and the source provides no per-capita adjustment.

This division's prison housing posture is distinguished in the source from one separate division, which is described as the only division maintaining separate facilities reserved for transgender people exclusively. This division's model is identity-based placement within the general population rather than a dedicated unit.

The July 2026 analysis sets this division's 1.9 recorded incidents against its 4.1 protective-law score to argue that statutory protection and recorded hostility coexist, which bears on how much weight a visitor should place on the division's legal posture when judging day-to-day exposure.

The shield statute of this division operates for families within this division and for families who travel to the state for care, protecting them from child-abuse investigations and criminal prosecution over gender-affirming care sought for a young person.

Transgender people held in the division's prisons are housed according to their gender identity within the general population under prison-service guidelines documented from 2015, and this division funds gender-affirming surgery for transgender inmates, a provision it introduced in 2015 as the first jurisdiction to do so.

This division recorded 198 of the more than 1,000 anti-LGBTQ incidents logged across the country in 2025, and its largest city saw a documented rise in anti-LGBTQ hate-crime reports to the police service over that period.

Whether the identity-based prison housing policy documented as of January 2021 remains in force is unresolved in this inventory; no source dated after that point confirms or contradicts it, and no trans-only facility in this division is documented either way.

The 198-incident figure for 2025 has no denominator in the sources, so its per-capita significance is unresolved; the ranking of sub-jurisdictions is by raw count only.

The methodology behind the July 2026 figures of a 4.1 law score and 1.9 recorded incidents is not stated in the inventory, including what the 1.9 counts or over what period.

No information specific to this division is sourced here on facility or bathroom access, identity-document and gender-marker rules, entry screening, or hate-crime statute coverage; those layers sit in the national record or are not covered by this inventory.

This division's anti-discrimination act prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity and gender expression in employment, housing, public accommodations, education and credit, a coverage in force since 2008 and expanded again by the 2025 legislature, as documented in the legislature's own 2025 summary of gender-affirming-care and transgender legislation.

Bill 1312 was signed by the governor on 16 May 2025 after passing on 6 May. It requires employers and schools to use a person's chosen name and pronouns, prohibits deadnaming and misgendering in workplaces and schools with immediate effect, and requires schools with dress codes to allow a student to choose from any uniform option. Its provisions simplifying changes of gender identity on birth certificates and driver's licences, and changes of name on marriage licences, take effect on 1 October 2026.

Gender markers on state documents are changeable without surgery. The board of the public health department removed the surgical requirement unanimously in February 2019, ending a rule that had applied since 1 January 1984. A change is made by request, using a Change of Sex Designation form to the motor vehicles agency for licences and IDs and Birth Certificate Correction and Sex Designation forms to the health department for birth certificates. Birth certificates offer M, F, Intersex and X markers; IDs and licences offer male, female and X. Minors need parent or guardian consent plus confirmation from a medical or mental health professional.

Facilities access is protected. In 2013 the civil rights division ruled that a transgender six-year-old child could use the girls' restroom at her elementary school in a town in this division, and in 2023 this division implemented a law granting full access to bathroom facilities for all genders. The state anti-bullying law prohibits bullying on the basis of gender identity and requires school districts to adopt prevention policies.

The hate-crime law has covered gender identity or expression since 2001, with penalty enhancements for bias-motivated crimes. In 2009 a jury in a city in this division convicted a man of first-degree murder with a hate-crime finding in a case described as the first murder trial applying a hate-crime law where the victim was transgender. The gay panic defence was abolished by a bipartisan bill passed in June 2020 and signed in July 2020, effective immediately.

Gender-affirming care is protected at state level but is under direct pressure. Legislation signed in April 2023 was enacted to protect, defend and guarantee gender-affirming healthcare services and to guarantee safe passage of transgender individuals from other jurisdictions. Since the beginning of 2023 basic health insurance coverage in this division must explicitly include sexual reassignment surgery as a basic policy, and a July 2026 assessment counts this division among jurisdictions with comprehensive health-insurance laws covering facial-hair removal and expanded gender-related coverage. On 18 May 2026 the highest civil court ruled 5-2 that a children's hospital in this division violated state anti-discrimination law when it suspended gender-affirming care for transgender youth under federal pressure, and ordered a lower court to issue an injunction requiring the hospital to resume puberty blockers and hormone therapy. One justice wrote that continuing such treatment for cisgender children while stopping it for transgender youth meant the decision denies the petitioners the full and equal enjoyment of services based on gender identity; two justices dissented, citing federal threats that could shut the hospital system.

Conversion therapy has been banned statewide on minors since a bill signed on 31 May 2019. After the highest civil court's 8-1 ruling of 31 March 2026 in a case requiring strict scrutiny of that ban, Bill 26-1322, passed on 8 May 2026, redefines conversion therapy as direction toward a pre-determined gender identity or sexual orientation outcome and removes the statute of limitations for claims.

Custody is governed by litigation rather than statute. A 2019 class action on behalf of transgender women held in men's prisons alleged that the prison service subjected them to sexual and physical violence and denied medically necessary care. The court-approved 2024 consent decree in a case, entered in a trial court in the division's principal city, required the prison service to expand health care, create voluntary specialised housing comprising a 100-bed unit at a men's facility in the division and an integration unit at the women's prison, and pay about $2.1 million to roughly 400 class members without admitting liability. A separate 2019 settlement paid a transgender inmate $170,000 over the safety of a transgender inmate held in a men's prison. No identity-based-housing statute governs placement in this division; trans women were historically held in men's prisons, with relief won through consent decree rather than a baseline housing rule.

Three ballot measures certified for the November 2026 vote would, if passed, write restrictions on transgender minors into this division's law. Initiative 109 would ban transgender children from gendered sports that do not align with their biological sex, and Initiative 110 would prohibit surgery on a child for the purpose of altering their sex characteristics; a third certified measure, Initiative 108, concerns child sex trafficking. The measures were pushed by conservative activists and signatures were certified by this division's elections officials on 17 March 2026.

Restrictions on transgender students in school sport have been adopted at district level. In April 2025 one district school board voted 3-2 to advance a policy banning biologically male students from female sports and the reverse; a second district board voted 6-1 in June 2025 for a similar policy, with a third district following suit. In December 2025 an undisclosed lawsuit settlement was reached over the banning of trans individuals from playing on female sports teams within some association governing districts, and the terms of that settlement are not public.

This division's protective framework is operating under direct funding pressure from this country's central government. The division's own health coverage agency has said that restoring coverage suspended under a central government rule will require legislative action, which indicates that division-level protection does not by itself hold when national funding conditions change. A visitor assessing this division should read its protections together with that constraint rather than as a fixed ceiling on what the division can deliver.

This division will suspend Medicaid coverage for hormone therapy, puberty blockers and other gender-affirming care for transgender youth beginning 13 October 2026, because a national rule finalised in August 2026 in this country blocks federal funds for such care for people under 18, and under 19 under a named child health programme. The division's Medicaid agency said resuming coverage will require legislative action by the legislature. About 500 youth under 19 received Medicaid-covered hormone therapy for gender dysphoria in fiscal 2024-25. Patients already taking hormones keep coverage through a six-month tapering period, and behavioural healthcare is unaffected.

The division's anti-bullying law requires school districts to adopt prevention policies covering bullying on the basis of gender identity, and schools with dress codes must allow any uniform option under a named act of the legislature. These are resident-facing obligations on school districts in this division rather than rules a visitor would encounter.

Implementation of the named act's document provisions is dated 1 October 2026, so changes of gender identity on birth certificates and driver's licences and changes of name on marriage licences in this division made before that date proceed under the earlier procedures.

The outcome of the November 2026 ballot measures is unresolved; two separate initiative measures were certified for the vote but their passage and any subsequent litigation are not sourced here.

The terms of the December 2025 lawsuit settlement concerning trans individuals barred from female sports teams in some association governing districts are undisclosed in the sources, so which districts are bound and on what terms remains unresolved.

Compliance with the 18 May 2026 order of this division's highest civil court is not sourced beyond the direction to a lower court to issue an injunction; whether the division's principal children's hospital resumed puberty blockers and hormone therapy, and whether other hospitals in this division altered care under pressure from this country's national government, is unresolved.

Whether the division's gender-recognition document-change provisions are operating as written after their 1 October 2026 effective date is not documented in the sources.

The status of the conversion-therapy regime after a legislative bill adopted in 2026, including any challenge to the redefined statute or to the strict-scrutiny standard set in a higher-court ruling on this point, is unresolved.

No division-specific figure for killings or violence against transgender people, measured against the general homicide rate in this division, appears in the sources; no such comparison can be made from this inventory.

The national layer, including passport and visa markers, entry screening, national custody policy and national care restrictions, is carried by this country's national record and is not restated here.

A bill, signed by the governor and effective 1 July 2026, makes it a crime for a transgender person to use a restroom or changing room that does not match the sex assigned at birth. It reaches government buildings and public-facing private businesses, including gas stations, restaurants, entertainment venues and hospitals. A first offence is a misdemeanour carrying up to one year in jail. A national civil-liberties organisation filed suit on 30 April 2026 on due-process, equal-protection and privacy grounds, arguing the law targets no criminal conduct; six transgender residents of this division are plaintiffs in the challenge, brought before the effect date. According to that organisation, this division's is the only law of its kind extending bathroom criminalisation to private businesses, and it carries steeper penalties than comparable bans elsewhere in this country.

The division's restroom statute is the only law of its kind in the parent country reaching private businesses, and a national civil liberties organisation assesses its penalties as steeper than comparable division-level bans. The division's continued X option on driver's licences and identity cards diverges from the position on national travel documents, so a visitor may hold a division-issued credential that does not match the marker available on a passport.

A 2022 bill passed by the lower house that would have imposed felony liability and up to life imprisonment on parents who took their children out of the division for gender-affirming care was blocked in the upper house. A bill passed by the lower house in February 2024 and pending in the upper house would recognise only male and female throughout this division's statutory code.

This division bars any change of sex on birth certificates, permitting only male or female sex at birth. The 2018 implementation law was allowed into legal effect in January 2026, ending a period from 6 April 2018 when transgender people could change birth certificates to reflect gender identity after a 2017 lawsuit. A 2020 statute that would have reversed that position was ruled moot and unenforceable on 7 August 2020 by a district judge, with $321,000 in attorneys' fees awarded to a legal advocacy organisation and approved in August 2022.

In November 2019 the health and welfare board removed doctor approval for a gender change for transgender minors, retaining parental permission, emancipation or a court order as the routes.

Transgender prisoners may receive hormone therapy under a September 2024 superior court ruling that nullified a 1997 law of this division banning it.

An April 2024 law bars teachers and education agencies from using pronouns for students that are not based on birth certificates. Transgender athletes are barred from public school and university teams matching their gender identity under legislation signed 30 March 2020. A March 2026 law requires schools, childcare providers and medical professionals to disclose a transgender minor's status to parents within three days of learning it.

County and city ordinances covering gender identity reach about 40% of the population: one county and thirteen cities listed in the source, plus employee protection in one further county.

Sources differ on the classification of the bathroom offence: a national civil liberties organisation describes a first offence as a misdemeanour carrying up to one year in jail, while one encyclopedia entry describes it as a felony. The discrepancy is unresolved.

Whether the 16 June 2026 narrowing by a judge of a federal district court remains in force, and the outcome of the suit brought by that national civil liberties organisation, are not established by the sources reviewed.

No record of enforcement action under the legislative provision on facilities access against a visitor or resident was identified in the sources reviewed.

No division-specific data on violence against transgender people that is materially above the general homicide rate in this division was identified in the sources reviewed.

The current litigation status of the 2018 birth-certificate implementation law is not sourced.

A division bill was enacted on 26 February 2026 when the legislature overrode the governor's veto, and it took effect immediately. The law confines transgender people to sex-segregated facilities matching sex assigned at birth in publicly owned buildings, a category a national advocacy organisation records as covering schools, universities, airports and government offices. It creates civil and criminal penalties of up to $1,000 for using a non-matching facility and authorises bounty-style lawsuits of at least $1,000 by any private person who claims to have shared a bathroom with a transgender person.

The same law bars the updating of driver's licences and state identification cards and invalidates existing licences whose gender marker is inconsistent with sex assigned at birth. The motor vehicle licensing agency has been mailing written notice, and many holders have already been told their licence is now invalid. Reissue is at the holder's expense with no grace period, and surrender letters warn of additional penalties for driving without a valid credential.

Two transgender men filed a court challenge in a trial court in this division within days of enactment, represented by a national civil liberties organisation and a private law firm, citing fear of violence under the facility-restriction and identification-invalidation provisions.

The identification rules rest on an earlier statute. That statute was enacted in April 2023 by veto override, defined biological sex in state law, and barred agencies from recognising genders beyond sex assigned at birth. The chief legal officer of this country then directed that new or updated driver's licences and birth certificates reflect only original sex at birth. A temporary restraining order barred gender-marker changes; an intermediate appeal court reversed unanimously on 13 June 2025 for lack of evidence of irreparable harm to law-enforcement identification; and in October 2025 the highest civil court rejected an appeal, allowing the motor vehicle licensing agency to continue the changes.

This division has prohibited discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations since 2020, following a 2020 decision of the highest court of this country and action by the division's anti-discrimination agency in August 2020 covering businesses with four or more employees. The division's hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by sexual orientation but does not cover gender identity; the law of this country has covered both since October 2009.

Marriage for same-sex couples became available after a federal judge ruled the division's ban unconstitutional on 4 November 2014, effective 12 November 2014, and became fully legal under a 2015 decision of the highest court of this country on 26 June 2015, with all judicial districts issuing licences by the end of that month. Consensual same-sex sexual activity is legal under a 2003 decision of the highest court of this country, which rendered this division's sodomy law unenforceable, though the legislature has not repealed its same-sex-only sodomy provisions carrying historic penalties of six months in jail and/or $1,000.

A trans-focused legal-risk assessment published on 20 February 2026 moved this division up from its mid-tier of adverse laws to the most severe travel-warning category, the first division added to that category in a year, citing the bathroom-bounty law that lets private individuals sue transgender people encountered in wrong-sex facilities. The assessment addresses exposure during interstate travel, meaning a visitor whose route passes through this division faces the same facility and identification rules as a resident.

The bounty provision is the operative enforcement mechanism: it does not depend on a state agency or prosecutor initiating action, since any private person can sue. That changes the practical exposure for a visitor using a public building, including an airport, during a trip.

This division banned transgender athletes from female school sports teams through a veto override in March 2023, effective 1 July 2023, after earlier bans passed in April 2021 and April 2022 were vetoed twice. The division's governing body for school sports, as of February 2023, left decisions case-by-case to schools.

Gender-affirming care for minors under 18 is banned. The head of the executive vetoed one bill on 12 April 2024 and the override failed by two votes; the executive vetoed a similar bill in February 2025 and that override succeeded on 18 February 2025. In May 2026 a judge in the division's trial court granted a temporary injunction blocking enforcement in a parental lawsuit backed by a national civil-liberties organisation.

Three municipalities banned conversion therapy on minors: one in June 2020, a second in April 2021 and a third in October 2021. In 2022 a middle-school teacher in one county of this division obtained a partial federal preliminary injunction allowing her to use students' non-preferred names and to disclose students' gender identity to parents despite a school preferred-name requirement.

Married same-sex couples may adopt. Lesbian couples may access in vitro fertilisation, with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognised only if married. The division permits gestational and traditional surrogacy on equal terms for same-sex and different-sex couples, but adoption agencies may refuse placements that violate their religious or moral convictions, and under a November 2012 adoption ruling and a court decision of 22 February 2013 unmarried non-biological partners obtain rights only in limited best-interest circumstances.

Sexual-orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations has been prohibited since 2020 under a ruling of this country's highest court and enforcement by the division's human rights commission, supplemented by city ordinances and executive orders issued in 2007, rescinded in 2015 and reissued in 2019. Voters in two municipalities repealed local ordinances on 6 November 2012. In March 2024 the legislature passed a law defining content containing "acts of homosexuality" as harmful to minors alongside pornography and requiring government ID-based age verification to access such material.

The outcome of Doe v. this country is unresolved; the suit was filed within days of this division's identification facility statute's enactment and no ruling is recorded in the sources.

Enforcement data for the statute's facility and identification provisions is not sourced. The number of licence holders who have received invalidation notices, and the number of bounty suits filed, are not recorded.

The division's hate-crime law's exclusion of gender identity is a statutory gap; whether this division's prosecution service charges such offences under the national law of this country is not documented in the sources.

An act enacted in this division in 2023 as a senate bill, protecting adolescents from experimental treatment, has been in force since 28 August 2023. It prohibits anyone under 18 from starting gender-affirming hormones or puberty blockers, allows those already in treatment to continue, and bans all transition-related surgery for minors. A state judge denied a preliminary injunction on 29 August 2023, and the statute took effect on schedule.

The same law bars this division's Medicaid programme from paying for gender-affirming care for a patient of any age, restricts treatment access in prisons, jails and correctional centres, and exposes providers who violate it to loss of their medical licence in this division and to patient lawsuits brought up to 15 years after treatment.

Litigation began with a complaint filed 25 July 2023 in a county circuit court by two national advocacy organisations and a law firm, acting for three families of transgender young people, medical providers, and two support organisations for families and clinicians. Following a trial in September 2024, a circuit judge upheld the ban on 25 November 2024 and the plaintiffs announced an appeal. The highest civil court of this division affirmed unanimously on 13 January 2026, quoting the 2025 ruling of the highest court of this country that upheld a comparable ban in a neighbouring jurisdiction. The statute sunsets in 2027, lawmakers have stated they want it made permanent, and a November 2026 ballot initiative seeks to bar such care indefinitely.

Care in custody is separately restricted. The governor signed a legislative bill, effective 2 July 2026, providing that no funds shall be expended for any cross-sex hormones or gender transition surgery undertaken for the purpose of any gender transition, with no taper plan for inmates already receiving care. This division became the seventh jurisdiction in this country to deny gender-affirming care to incarcerated people and the second in 2026 to do so. Three other jurisdictions have near-identical laws, while comparable measures in two further jurisdictions were blocked by federal courts.

Trans athletes are barred from female sports. A senate bill, signed 7 June 2023, requires public and private schools through college to restrict sports participation to sex assigned at birth; the ban carries a sunset clause repealing it automatically on 28 August 2027.

Identity documents carry a surgical requirement. A change of sex on a birth certificate issued in this division requires a court order with certified proof on hospital letterhead, signed by the attending physician with licence and contact details, stating that the petitioner's physical sex has been altered and the surgical changes are irreversible, under a numbered provision of this division's annotated statutes. Two 2013 cases that had permitted an exception were invalidated and reversed in May 2022, leaving no route around the surgical requirement. The licensing agency accepted a standard form for changing the gender designation on a licence or ID after policy review between 2016 and 2024, then reverted to requiring surgery documentation or a court order after an unspecified incident.

Protection machinery is uneven. This division's hate crime statutes explicitly cover gender identity, defined as "having a self-image or identity not traditionally associated with one's gender," while state non-discrimination legislation does not address gender identity at all.

This division's care ban for incarcerated people belongs to a wider division-level pattern: seven divisions now deny gender-affirming care to inmates, and this division is the second to enact such a measure in 2026. Court outcomes diverge sharply by jurisdiction, with near-identical statutes standing in three other divisions of this country and comparable measures in two further divisions blocked by the parent country's courts.

The chief legal officer of this division issued emergency orders in March and April 2023 declaring gender-affirming care experimental. The adult-care order, set to expire February 2024, would have required three years of documented intense dysphoria, at least 15 psychiatric sessions over 18 months with at least 10 with the same therapist, treatment of comorbidities, autism screening, 15-year adverse-effect tracking, annual dysphoria assessment, screening for social contagion, written consent every three months for three years and detailed compliance records. A judge temporarily blocked it and the chief legal officer withdrew it in May 2023, along with the parallel youth-care orders of March and April 2023.

The direction of travel in the legislature runs toward permanence rather than expiry: the 2027 sunset of this division's statute was a partisan concession at enactment, and both lawmakers and a November 2026 ballot initiative are now moving to remove it.

Before the 2022 reversal, two 2013 cases had allowed a birth-certificate change without the surgical certification; their invalidation closed the only documented workaround, so the current document rule is stricter in practice than the statute alone suggests.

This division has no state law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of gender identity. The only related instrument is a 2010 executive order providing sexual-orientation protections for government employees; a legislature-passed bill banning sexual-orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations passed 19-11 in 2013 and died when the lower chamber adjourned without considering it.

The state operates a tipline for anonymous reporting of suspected violations of the care ban and for general complaints about a "gender transition intervention."

The largest city in this division declared itself a sanctuary city for transgender individuals and rights in May 2023, and a second city voted in February 2024 to include LGBT protections in its sanctuary ordinance.

This division has no law limiting adoption on the basis of LGBT status under its adoption statute at § 453.010, with no explicit prohibition on same-sex or second-parent adoption. Domestic partnership registries in one suburb, two further cities, one county, and a university district grant certain benefits within their borders to both opposite- and same-sex couples.

In August 2021, a state bill reformed the division's 1980s-era HIV criminalisation laws, reducing the offence from a felony to a misdemeanor.

The sources date the denial of the preliminary injunction against the challenged act differently: one report places it on 29 August 2023, another in August 2024. The discrepancy is unresolved here.

Whether the funding bar in the bill under review reaches pre-trial detainees as well as sentenced prisoners is not stated in the sources.

The revenue department's reversal of its gender-marker form policy is attributed only to an "unspecified incident"; no date, internal guidance or legal challenge to the reverted policy is documented, and whether the current requirement has been litigated is unresolved.

The sources contain no dated incident of violence against a trans person in this division, with an outcome, so no such incident can be stated. They also provide no figure for this division covering trans people held in state custody.

Whether the 2027 sunset of the challenged act will be extended by legislation and what the November 2026 ballot initiative yields are unresolved.

No rule specific to this division governing airport screening or entry inspection of trans travellers appears in the sources; any such exposure would arise under federal rather than state authority.

This division's state-level framework for trans visitors is set by Executive Order No. 23-16, signed by the governor on 30 August 2023. The order establishes a Women's Bill of Rights and defines sex, female, male, woman, girl, man, boy, mother and father for use by state agencies, stating that biological sex is determined at birth and that biological differences between males and females in athletic ability and safety warrant sex-based segregation in some athletic, social and educational spaces. The order backs single-sex spaces for women's sports, bathrooms and changing rooms. The governor was the second in this country to sign such an order. Opponents questioned the order's scope and legality.

State documents are correspondingly restrictive. A legal gender marker change on a birth certificate of this division requires a notarized affidavit from the physician who performed sex reassignment surgery together with a certified copy of a court order changing the applicant's name. A driver's licence or state ID change requires a court order certifying the change and/or a physician-signed form confirming sex reassignment surgery. A name change requires district court paperwork, a court date, and publication for four consecutive weeks, or two weeks for minors. These requirements apply to state-issued documents; a visitor holding an out-of-state or foreign passport is not directly governed by them, but a trans person resident in this division or seeking identification issued here faces them.

Participation rules for trans students in this division's athletics have tightened in stages. The schools athletics association requires transgender students to show evidence of hormone replacement therapy and/or sex reassignment surgery. In June 2025 Legislative Bill 89, banning transgender athletes from any sports, passed the unicameral legislature by a two-thirds majority and was signed by the governor; ten transgender athletes were identified as affected.

Gender-affirming healthcare for people under 19 is barred in this division. The legislature passed the ban 33-15 in May 2023 and the governor signed it effective immediately. The highest civil court upheld it 6-1 in July 2024. A trans visitor under 19 cannot obtain this care in this division, and a visitor of any age cannot obtain it for a minor in their care.

Custody is a documented site of harm specific to this division. A transgender woman diagnosed with gender dysphoria and transitioning while held in this division's men's prison sued prison officials and workers; on 10 August 2022 a federal district judge ruled for the defendants, dismissing her claims of failure to treat her dysphoria, denial of gender-conforming surgery, and failure to protect her. The division had housed her by assigned sex at birth among male prisoners and placed her in a cell with a convicted male sex offender who sexually assaulted her. The judge had earlier dismissed the failure-to-protect claim over that placement, wrote that without medical evidence no reasonable jury could conclude the providers were deliberately indifferent to her serious medical need, and said she had not plausibly alleged more than de minimis injuries from the assault. He found no support for inferring a substantial risk from a prospective cellmate's sexual-offence conviction coupled with the alleged vulnerability of a transgender inmate transitioning to a woman in a men's prison. The placement followed her within the system.

Protection machinery is uneven. This division's 1997 hate crime law guarantees the right to live free from violence or intimidation by threat of violence and enhances sentences for manslaughter, assault, terroristic threats, stalking, kidnapping and false imprisonment, rape and sexual assault, arson, criminal mischief and trespassing. It does not address gender identity. Federal law has covered gender identity under a national hate crimes prevention statute since 2009. The highest civil court upheld the hate crime law in April 2016, in a case protecting even a straight victim in the company of gay friends.

Discrimination protection for trans people in this division rests on federal rulings and municipal ordinances rather than statewide statute. Employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity became illegal under a national supreme court ruling decided 15 June 2020. In August 2020 the state equal opportunity commission announced it would investigate and resolve housing discrimination claims on account of sexual orientation or gender identity, applying the same ruling to housing. Federal enforcement followed: from 11 February 2021 the federal fair housing prohibition on discrimination because of sex was enforced to include sexual orientation and gender identity, with the national housing agency accepting, investigating and enforcing complaints of anti-trans housing discrimination covering sale, rental, terms, conditions and services. The largest city in this division has prohibited discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment and public accommodations in both the public and private sectors since 2012, when the city council voted 4-3 on 13 March to amend the city's anti-discrimination laws to add sexual orientation and gender identity as protected classes, with an exemption for religious institutions. The second city passed a 5-0 ordinance in February 2022 covering employment, accommodation and housing, but the protections were removed in June 2022 after a petition drive. In November 2021 the state college system voted 4-2 to include gender identity in its policy.

Conversion therapy aimed at changing gender identity is outlawed in that second city under a 2021 ordinance and remains lawful in the rest of this division. Statewide ban bills were reintroduced in 2021 and 2025 but have not passed.

Marriage and family recognition are settled in this division as a matter of federal law. Same-sex marriage has been legal under a national supreme court ruling of 26 June 2015, with the then state attorney general directing compliance and non-enforcement of contrary state laws. That replaced a constitutional ban adopted in November 2000 by 70 per cent to 30 per cent defining marriage as the union of a man and a woman. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can marry and have that marriage recognised. This division permits adoption by same-sex couples and single LGBT individuals: a district court ruled for the plaintiffs in an adoption case on 5 August 2015, the highest civil court upheld that ruling in April 2017 striking down the ban on same-sex foster parents, and in March 2021 it held that state adoption law clearly allows a same-sex married couple to adopt.

Sodomy prohibitions in this division were repealed by a revised criminal code enacted in June 1977, effective 1 July 1978, by a veto override of 32-15 against the governor.

The practical weight of this division's state measures depends on how long a visitor stays and what they need from state institutions. A short-stay visitor using only federal documents and private accommodation encounters the state framework mainly through facilities practice and the absence of a statewide gender-identity discrimination statute. A trans person resident in this division, or a visitor needing division-issued identification or care, meets the marker requirements, the under-19 care ban and the athletics rules directly.

A trans visitor in a relationship that this division's authorities would read as same-sex under birth-sex status has full marriage and adoption recognition, so the usual concern about partner recognition in hostile jurisdictions does not arise here. The exposure lies elsewhere: in facilities, in custody if arrested and held in state or local detention, and in the absence of a statewide hate-crime or anti-discrimination provision naming gender identity.

Enforcement of the 1997 hate crime law is documented in a case the highest civil court decided in April 2016 protecting a straight victim in the company of gay friends, which indicates the statute is applied to perceived-association bias, but nothing in this division's own law extends that to gender identity. National protection under this country's federal hate-crimes prevention statute covers gender identity, so a bias-motivated offence against a trans person can be charged federally even where state law is silent.

A trans person changing identification while living in this division works through procedures that assume surgical intervention. Birth certificate amendment requires a notarized physician affidavit confirming sex reassignment surgery plus a certified court order changing the name. Driver's licence and state ID changes require a court order certifying the change and/or a physician-signed form confirming sex reassignment surgery. A name change runs through district court paperwork, a hearing date, and newspaper publication for four consecutive weeks, or two weeks for minors.

Gender-affirming care for anyone under 19 is banned. The 2023 law passed the legislature 33-15, was signed effective immediately, and was upheld by the highest state court 6-1 in July 2024. A resident trans minor, or a parent seeking care for one, has no lawful in-state route.

Employment and housing claims on gender identity rest on federal law. A federal court decision of 15 June 2020 made gender-identity employment discrimination illegal. The state civil rights agency began investigating housing discrimination claims on sexual orientation and gender identity in August 2020, and from 11 February 2021 the federal housing agency enforced the federal fair housing law's sex provision to cover sexual orientation and gender identity, accepting and investigating complaints covering sale, rental, terms, conditions and services. Local ordinances add coverage in one large city, which has protected gender identity in employment and public accommodations in the public and private sectors since March 2012, with a religious-institution exemption. Another city's February 2022 ordinance covering employment, accommodation and housing was removed by petition in June 2022. The state college system added gender identity to its policy by a 4-2 vote in November 2021.

Conversion therapy on gender identity is prohibited in one city under a 2021 ordinance and lawful elsewhere in the division; statewide ban bills in 2021 and 2025 did not pass.

Trans students in this division's school athletics must show evidence of hormone replacement therapy and/or sex reassignment surgery under state school activities association rules, and a bill signed by the governor in June 2025 after passing two-thirds of the legislature bars transgender athletes from any sports; ten athletes were identified as affected.

Incarceration practice follows assigned sex at birth. In August 2022 a federal judge dismissed a transgender woman's claims of failure to treat dysphoria, denial of gender-conforming surgery and failure to protect her after she was housed among male prisoners and celled with a convicted male sex offender who assaulted her. The ruling treated the assault injuries as no more than de minimis and found no inference of substantial risk from the cellmate's prior sex-offence conviction combined with her vulnerability as a transitioning woman in a men's prison.

The report from a national news publisher on the head of the executive signing Executive Order No. 23-16 could not be retrieved; the publisher returns a 403 error to automated fetches. Its content is corroborated by that office's own press release, a legal-affairs outlet's report and local coverage, so the underlying facts are not in doubt, but the article text itself was not read.

The inventory does not record this division's measures on bathroom access beyond Executive Order No. 23-16's endorsement of single-sex spaces, does not record whether any city in this division or the division itself has adopted a facility-use enforcement provision, and does not record division-level statistics on violence against trans people in this division. No figure for trans homicide or assault victimisation in this division is sourced here, so none is stated.

Several provisions in the countrywide layer are in litigation or have been enjoined, and the operative position on those countrywide measures should be checked before travel. That layer is carried by the countrywide record.

The inventory does not record this division's current rules on gender markers for division-issued documents after the 2023 executive order, so whether any division agency has narrowed marker practice beyond the statutory surgery requirements described here is unresolved on the sources reviewed.

As of July 2026 this division is listed among the most protective in this country on gender-identity nondiscrimination. Division law bans discrimination based on gender identity in employment, public accommodations, education, housing, credit, insurance and union practices. The provision was added after a 2006 veto, passed again in 2007, was signed by the governor on 22 May 2007 and took effect on 1 July 2007. For a visitor the public-accommodations coverage is the operative part: hotels, restaurants, shops and service providers fall under it.

Hate-crime law provides additional penalties for an offence committed because of the victim's gender identity, added in 1999 to a 1990 statute that originally covered sexual orientation. The gay and trans panic defence was abolished and repealed by legislation that passed the lower chamber of the legislature 144-1 in March 2021 and the upper chamber 29-0 in April 2021, was signed by the governor on 5 May 2021 and took effect on 1 July 2021.

Single-user public bathrooms have had to be marked gender-neutral since 1 July 2018, under a bill signed in May 2018.

The division's shield laws, enacted in 2023 and 2024, are enforceable against out-of-state action and place it among those protecting transgender and non-binary people who travel in for gender-affirming healthcare; the 2023 measure took effect immediately by emergency clause.

Partner recognition is settled. Civil unions were introduced in July 2000 as the first such status identical to marriage in any division of this country, following a 1999 ruling of this division's highest court on equal marriage benefits, and marriage for same-sex couples has been legal since 1 September 2009, the first division in this country to adopt it through the legislature and governor rather than a court decision.

This division's sexual-orientation protections run alongside the gender-identity provisions and predate them. Discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, public accommodations, education, housing, credit, insurance and union practices was banned with protections added in 1992; hate-crime legislation covering sexual orientation was enacted in 1990; and benefits for same-sex partners of public-sector employees have been provided since 1994.

This division's sodomy statutes are repealed. The penalty was reduced from capital punishment to life imprisonment in 1861; a 1937 law punished participation in oral sex with one to five years in state prison and applied to heterosexual and homosexual activity alike; that statute was repealed in April 1977; and adult private consensual non-commercial sodomy is unenforceable under a ruling of the highest civil court of this country.

Gender-marker changes on this division's birth certificates and other state-issued documents are available to both preoperative and postoperative transgender people on court order, supported by a letter from a licensed medical or mental health practitioner documenting surgical, hormonal or other appropriate treatment. Since 1 July 2022, people born in this division may change the sex marker to male, female or X by self-determination, without court order, mental health diagnosis, surgery, divorce or medical permission, under legislation approved 6 April 2022, which amended the relevant statute governing vital records to allow issuance of a new birth certificate reflecting gender identity.

The motor vehicle agency has offered X on driver's licences and state IDs since 1 July 2019, with no documentation required.

Health insurers underwriting in this division have been required to cover transgender care, including sex reassignment surgery, since 2013.

Conversion therapy on minors, including transgender minors, is prohibited. Legislation was signed on 25 May 2016 and took effect on 1 July 2016, treating performance of the practice on minors as unprofessional conduct under the relevant health and safety code sections and related professional licensing statutes. The bill passed the upper chamber unanimously on 17 March 2016, was approved with amendments in the lower chamber on 26 April and accepted by the upper chamber on 29 April.

Adoption and parentage rules are open to LGBT residents. Single LGBT individuals and same-sex couples may petition to adopt; lesbian couples have access to in vitro fertilisation, with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognised as legal parent of a child born via donor insemination irrespective of marital status; and in June 1993 the highest civil court ruled in favour of a lesbian seeking to adopt her partner's two biological sons.

The anti-bullying law prohibits bullying, including cyberbullying, and harassment based on gender identity and sexual orientation in all educational institutions. In October 2023 the education department unanimously passed a policy to protect and defend transgender and non-binary students within schools and classrooms. In 2023 one private school's girls' basketball team forfeited a match against a team fielding a transgender girl, citing fairness and safety, and the body governing school sports barred it from competition as a result.

The sources do not itemise the provisions of the 2024 shield law; the inventory records only that shield laws were enacted in 2023 and 2024 and are enforceable against out-of-state action.

No enforcement data specific to this division is present in the sources for the gender-identity hate-crime provision or for complaints brought under the public-accommodations statute, so the practical operation of those protections is not sourced here.

Whether the 2022 self-determination rule extends to state-issued documents beyond birth certificates is not specified in the sources; the driver's licence and state ID marker is governed separately by the 2019 motor-vehicle policy.

This division operates within the federal framework of this country, and the national layer of exposure is carried in the country assessment. Division law protects gender identity across several areas a visitor encounters directly, while this division's transgender-related restrictions are concentrated in schools and in rules covering minors.

A non-discrimination statute passed 6 February 2020, signed 11 April 2020 and effective 1 July 2020, prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations and credit. It covers sexual orientation on the same terms and replaced earlier protections limited to public-sector employment. A law signed 4 March 2020 with the same effective date authorises localities to enact their own sexual-orientation and gender-identity protections.

Violence motivated by gender identity falls within this division's hate crime law under legislation signed 4 March 2020 and effective 1 July 2020, which also added sexual orientation. A bill repealing the gay and trans panic defence, passed in March 2021, was signed by the governor, and took effect on 1 July 2021.

State identity documents are comparatively accessible. An X gender marker has been offered on driver's licences since 1 July 2020, and since 1 September 2020 changing the sex designation on a birth certificate requires only "appropriate clinical treatment", replacing a surgery requirement that had been in force since 1979.

Criminal provisions on private sexual conduct no longer stand. A codified section on consensual adult sexual conduct was struck down on 12 March 2013 and revised to remove the criminalisation of consensual same-sex relations, by an upper-chamber vote of 40-0 on 7 February 2014 and a lower-chamber vote of 100-0 on 6 March 2014, signed into immediate effect. A section on lewd cohabitation was repealed in 2013 and a section on fornication was repealed on 4 March 2020. The relevant statutes had already been rendered unenforceable by a 2003 decision of this country's highest court.

Marriage between people of the same sex is recognised in this division and has been performed since 6 October 2014, when this country's highest court declined to hear the appeal in a named case and marriages began at 1 p.m. that day. The statutory ban was repealed on 3 March 2020, and a codifying protection was signed in March 2024, effective 1 July. The 2006 constitutional amendment banning such marriages remains in the constitution, with repeal resolutions approved in January 2025 and January 2026 awaiting a voter referendum. A designated-visitor statute signed 26 March 2007 and effective 1 July 2007 extended hospital visitation rights to same-sex couples.

On schools, in 2014 a county school board was held to have acted unlawfully in denying a transgender high school student use of the boys' bathroom, a ruling this country's highest court allowed to stand in 2021. In July 2023 the division's education department adopted policies banning bathroom access and pronoun usage for transgender students, which were intended to be reversed in 2026. The state school sports governing body barred transgender athletes from girls' sports in February 2025. This division prohibits health care providers from attempting to change the gender identity of minors.

Official posture toward transgender students has moved in both directions through the courts. In September 2021 this division's highest court upheld the reinstatement of a teacher suspended for speaking against transgender children and declining to use their pronouns on grounds of Christian belief. In May 2024 the governor vetoed a bullying-definition bill that would have included gender identity.

A July 2026 legal risk assessment places this division in a named group alongside eight other divisions and a federal district, and names this division and one other division as jurisdictions that have enacted youth-targeting anti-trans policies which, on that assessment's reading of jurisdiction-specific factors, appear unlikely to extend to adults.

The division-level document position does not align with the national travel-document position described at country level: a visitor may hold a driver's licence or birth certificate issued in this division carrying markers that the national passport regime no longer issues, and the two layers have to be read separately.

This division's protections for gender identity were enacted by statute in 2020 and by the panic-defence repeal in 2021. Its restrictions on transgender students, by contrast, were adopted administratively by the department of education in July 2023 and by the schools' sports governing body in February 2025, and the school policies were intended for reversal in 2026.

Family formation rules matter mainly to residents. Single people may adopt in this division with no explicit prohibition on same-sex couples adopting, but HB 189 and SB 349, signed 9 April 2012 and effective 1 July 2012, authorise adoption agencies to refuse on religious grounds. A bill passed in February 2019, signed in March 2019 and effective 1 July 2019 legalised surrogacy contracts for same-sex couples, and a February 2021 bill barred taxpayer funds from going to religious organisations that discriminate in adoption.

Health-related provisions affecting residents include the prohibition on providers attempting to change the sexual orientation of minors, alongside the ban on attempts to change a minor's gender identity, and SB 1138, signed 31 March 2021, which decriminalised and modernised this division's HIV laws. A bill barring insurance discrimination against PrEP users was vetoed in March 2025.

A state-by-state list of bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity is attributed in the research to an external equality map maintained by a named advocacy organisation, but the URL cited for it now returns HTTP 404 after the page moved, and the list could not be verified at the cited address.

Several points remain unresolved. Whether the July 2023 federal education department policies have in fact been reversed is not established in the available sources. Removal of the 2006 constitutional marriage ban depends on a voter referendum for which no date is sourced. The conclusion that this division's youth-targeting policies are unlikely to extend to adults is a risk assessment based on division-specific factors, not a court ruling. No division-specific figures on hate-crime enforcement or on violence against transgender people appear in the available sources.

This division operates under the national framework of this country on passports, entry screening, federal facilities and federal custody, which are set nationally. Division law and division institutions govern health care, insurance, the division prison system and division ballot measures.

A July 2026 legal-risk assessment of this country's anti-trans measures places this division among the most protective divisions in the country. The same assessment flags two division ballot initiatives, I-001 and I-638, due for a November vote, as targeting transgender residents; whether they pass decides whether that protective posture holds.

This division has shield laws or executive orders from the 2023 and 2024 batches that are enforceable against out-of-jurisdiction action, and a nationwide tracker of such measures lists this division among those covered. For a trans visitor who travels to this division for gender-affirming care, these measures bear on whether action taken by another division can reach care provided in this division.

Division correctional practice carries a documented reversal. Prisons in this division have been legally required since October 2023, under court order and rulings, to provide gender-affirming healthcare and, where indicated, sex-reassignment surgery to inmates. In July 2024 a transgender woman prisoner was transferred out of a women's prison back to a men's prison as punishment for consensual sex with a cisgender inmate of the women's prison, so housing assigned by birth sex functioned as the disciplinary sanction.

The July 2026 assessment lists this division among four divisions with comprehensive health-insurance laws covering facial hair removal and an expanded range of gender-affirming procedures, alongside three neighbouring divisions.

The protection is at division level and coexists with a restrictive federal layer. Shield-law protection does not change federal rules on passports, entry, federal custody or federal facilities, and both operate at once for anyone in this division.

State law requires health insurance to cover facial hair removal and an expanded range of gender-affirming procedures, a coverage set the July 2026 assessment identifies in only four divisions. Residents receive that coverage regardless of where the care is sought under the shield measures.

This division extends refugee protections to people leaving divisions with hostile regimes, as recorded in the same assessment.

The text and current status of ballot initiatives I-001 and I-638 are not sourced; the inventory records only that they target transgender residents and are due for a November vote.

The inventory does not specify whether this division's shield measure is a statute or an executive order, whether it dates from the 2023 or the 2024 batch, or what enforcement record exists under it.

Whether the use of birth-sex housing as a disciplinary placement in July 2024 continued in this division's prisons after that year is not sourced.

The content of this division's refugee protections, and how a person qualifies for them, is not in the inventory.

This division stands under the national federal framework of this country; the national layer is carried on the national record rather than repeated here.

A national legal risk assessment published in July 2026 places this division in its Low-Risk group alongside eight other divisions, describing that group as jurisdictions that have largely refrained from targeting transgender adults. The same assessment names this division together with one other division as a jurisdiction whose youth-targeting anti-trans policies are judged unlikely to be extended to adults.

Employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity is prohibited in this division through 2020 federal appeals-court rulings under Title VII covering sexual orientation and gender identity, reinforced by a January 2023 gubernatorial executive order banning gender-identity discrimination in state employment and contracts and a June 2023 statement by the chief legal officer affirming that state sex discrimination includes gender identity. Municipal ordinances in nine municipalities (revised February 2013, March 2013, February 2014, 2015, November 2018, March 2021, April 2021 effective 20 May, May 2021 and June 2021) ban gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations, with exemptions for religious organizations, expressive groups, government agencies, private clubs and small businesses.

The division's hate-crime statute does not include gender identity, though a federal hate-crimes prevention act has covered gender identity since October 2009. A gay and trans panic defence remains available under common law, with reform bills lapsing without action.

Gender-affirming care for minors is restricted. A March 2022 law signed by the governor banned sex reassignment surgery on transgender children effective March 2023, with an exception permitting surgery on intersex children. A 1982 regulation bars public medical-assistance coverage of sex reassignment surgery; that ban was challenged in August 2020 by two transgender teenagers with national civil-rights and health-law co-counsel as unconstitutional, following 2019 lawsuits seeking to void it. A June 2023 executive order granted government employees over age 21 full public medical-assistance and insurance coverage for gender-affirming healthcare and services. Conversion therapy was banned in one county in August 2017 by a 3-2 vote with fines up to $2,500, alongside a June 2023 executive order barring government funding for conversion therapy.

The division's highest court ruled on 25 April 2019 that family courts may determine care for a transgender child with gender dysphoria only in limited circumstances when divorced parents reach impasse, authorized to decide disputed parenting-plan elements narrowly tailored on evidence of imminent harm. In March 2023 the division's education department introduced a hotline to report schools exposing children to topics including gender ideology for investigation. In June 2023 the governor vetoed legislature-passed anti-trans bathroom and classroom pronoun-usage bills and vetoed an April 2023 bill targeting LGBT safe spaces in schools.

A second March 2022 bill signed by the governor legally bars transgender children from female sports, athletics and Olympic competition, effective 30 days after enactment.

Birth certificates and driver's licences carry distinct rules. In November 2020 three families with transgender children sued the division's health authority to permit birth-certificate gender change without sex reassignment surgery; litigation was ongoing as of August 2023 with all resident transgender individuals joined, and an August 2024 federal judge order permitted change without surgery. Driver's licence and state ID gender change requires a signed physician statement attesting the applicant is irrevocably committed to the gender-change process, without requiring surgery.

Same-sex marriage has been recognized since a federal district court decision on 17 October 2014 ended enforcement of statutory and constitutional bans, though those bans remain textually in the division's constitution and statutory code as unenforceable under a 2015 highest-court marriage-equality ruling and, for out-of-state recognition, a 2022 federal marriage-recognition act. Voters rejected a 2006 ballot measure and approved a 2008 ballot measure banning recognition, prompting four municipalities to enact domestic partnerships or civil unions.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal after a 2001 repeal statute did away with sodomy laws. Adoption is permitted with no explicit prohibition on same-sex couples or second-parent adoptions, though primary consideration goes to married couples unless in the child's best interest or no married couple is available; the division's highest court ruled unanimously in September 2017 that same-sex spouses have equal parental rights under the 2015 marriage-equality ruling and a subsequent highest-court ruling to list both names on birth certificates, with October 2020 appeals implementation. Surrogacy contracts are unenforceable though a 1994 state appellate ruling allows pre-birth orders for biological parents requiring second-parent adoption for a non-biological same-sex parent, and an April 2022 emergency law signed by the governor allows religious organizations to legally discriminate against same-sex couples seeking to adopt or foster.

On 3 June 2026 a national monitoring project reported that the local pride organisation cancelled all 2026 events in January and effectively dissolved, citing a political and financial environment that made supporting queer events nearly impossible; that city was grouped with two cities in other divisions of this country as affected cities.
